document.group: PJM governance and stakeholder reform vote

pages.text:
1 
 
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms  
  
Docket No. AD26-7-000  
 
PRE-TECHNICAL CONFERENCE COMMENTS OF 
THE PSEG COMPANIES 
 
The PSEG Companies1 appreciate the opportunity to submit these comments in advance of 
the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“Commission”) 2026 Technical Conference on 
PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms (“Technical Conference”) to be held on July 23, 
2026.  These comments address the issues to be discussed during Panel 2: “PJM Stakeholder 
Process–Design, Transparency, and Decision-Making.” This panel will examine the PJM 
stakeholder process, the flaws inherent in this process and ways to fix, or at least mitigate, these 
challenges. PSEG recognizes the Commission’s leadership in convening this technical 
conference.  This timely and needed initiative comes when PJM is at an inflection point in its 
history, grappling with how to address the region’s profound resource adequacy challenge before 
it becomes a major reliability crisis for customers across the region. As both a founding member 
and significant Transmission Owner (“TO”) in PJM, PSEG offers a unique and informed 
perspective on PJM’s flawed governance structure. Fixing PJM governance is not optional, and 
there are a range of potential solutions. Fundamentally, the objective must be to achieve 
consistently better, durable outcomes at PJM – defined as supporting (i) a system that is reliably 
planned in the short-term and in the long-term and a well-functioning wholesale electricity 
market with stable, defensible rules; (ii) efficient and timely decision-making; and (iii) an RTO 
 
1 The PSEG Companies are Public Service and Gas Company (“PSE&G”), PSEG Power LLC and PSEG Energy 
Resources & Trade LLC, which are each wholly-owned, direct or indirect subsidiaries of Public Service Enterprise 
Group Incorporated (“PSEG”) (collectively, “PSEG” or the “PSEG Companies”).  PSEG is a diversified energy 
company based in Newark, New Jersey consisting primarily of a regulated electric and gas utility and a nuclear 
generation business.  Through its wholly-owned subsidiary PSE&G, PSEG owns over 2,200 circuit miles of electric 
transmission lines within the PJM region.  PSE&G has 2.4 million electric customers in its franchised service 
territory and an obligation to reliably serve those customers.  For 24 consecutive years, PSE&G has won reliability 
awards in the Mid-Atlantic region and has a proven record of providing reliable and affordable service to customers.  
PSEG also has an ownership interest in approximately 3,800 MW of reliable, baseload nuclear generation.

2 
 
that is both empowered to make the right decisions and is fully accountable for those decisions. 
PSEG proposes actionable solutions to deliver these results.  
This is not an academic exercise; customer reliability is at risk. Just this year, due to the 
unsolved supply/demand imbalance, PJM has gone into emergency alert conditions across the 
region four times, and in the process has sought and obtained multiple emergency authorizations 
from the Department of Energy (“DOE”) permitting it to run generating units beyond otherwise-
applicable permit limitations and to call on large customers to run back-up generation, subject to 
curtailment if necessary.2 This continual state of operating in “crisis mode” is not sustainable. 
  PSEG has had iron in the ground in PJM for decades. Our core concerns, and stake in the 
future of PJM, do not – and will not - wax and wane based on individual Regional Transmission 
Expansion Plan (“RTEP”) cycles or Base Residual Auctions. We have warned of critical flaws in 
PJM governance for years, and unfortunately those risks have fully materialized. We are deeply 
committed to continuing to work with PJM to keep the lights on for our customers. Our 
comments are offered through this lens and with this long-term perspective.  
 
I. 
Executive Summary 
PJM’s governance model is broken. As Chairman Laura Swett stated at the May 2026 PJM 
Annual Meeting, the “current stakeholder process is slow where it must be fast, opaque where it 
must be transparent, and vulnerable to vetoes and agenda control exactly when the region needs 
immediate action.”3  While it may seem counterintuitive to tackle PJM governance while PJM 
and its stakeholders are simultaneously seeking to solve the substantive issues of large load 
integration and resource adequacy, the reality is that the flawed governance structure has (i) 
played a role in causing these problems and (ii) will prevent PJM and its stakeholders from 
developing effective, long-term solutions. The current process is locked in an endless cycle of 
finger pointing, lack of defined accountabilities, flawed voting and contentious stakeholder 
processes -- with no resolution in sight.  
 
2 NERC EEA conditions were announced January 26, 2026; May 17 to 19, 2026; June 30 to July 2, 2026; and July 
14 to July 21, 2026.  See Emergency Procedures - Postings. 
3 See Chairman Laura Swett's Comments at PJM's Annual Meeting in Baltimore, MD | Federal Energy Regulatory 
Commission.

3 
 
PJM is fundamentally different from other RTOs and ISOs. ISO-NE, for example, consists of 
six states that have relatively homogenous state policies. MISO and SPP, while representing 
large footprints, consist primarily of vertically integrated states. New York and California are 
single state ISOs, minimizing regional policy friction that affects multi-state markets. By 
contrast, PJM is comprised of fourteen jurisdictions with a large range of state policies reflected 
in the vast membership, and a combination of retail choice and vertically integrated states. PJM’s 
vast size, broad scope and regional diversity exacerbate its governance challenges.  
The fundamental flaws in PJM’s governance structure were largely masked over the past two 
decades because the relevant externalities were significantly different. During most of that time, 
PJM was in a position of excess supply and demand was manageable and somewhat predictable, 
with largely flat or declining load growth. Under surplus capacity conditions PJM’s governance 
was not truly stress-tested. With economics and policy causing the retirement of a significant 
amount of capacity in the region4 and the recent rapid demand growth driven by the integration 
of large loads,5 the externalities have now radically changed, and PJM’s governance problems 
have been fully exposed.   
PJM acknowledges this reality in its recently issued whitepaper on market design reforms, 
“Powering Reliability Through Market Design.”6 As noted by PJM President and CEO David 
Mills, “the conditions that made the market work for nearly two decades have changed.”7  Mills 
explains that the problems facing the region are “more fundamental than a design that needs 
recalibration” and that “the current situation is not tenable.”8 These statements are 
simultaneously revealing and troubling. 
We are not interested in assigning blame as that is neither productive nor fair.  Instead, we 
seek to be a constructive partner in resolving the governance issues that lie before us. PJM has 
 
4 See Monitoring Analytics, "2023 State of the Market Report for PJM," Section 1 Introduction, page 1. Document 
file: 2023-som-pjm-sec1.pdf, available at: https://monitoringanalytics.com. 
5 See PJM 2026 PJM Load Forecast Report (Jan. 14, 2026) (available at: https://www.pjm.com/-
/media/DotCom/library/reports-notices/load-forecast/2026-load-report.pdf). 
6 See PJM Whitepaper entitled "Powering Reliability Through Market Design," (May 6, 2026) (“PJM 2026 
Whitepaper”) available at: https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/library/reports-notices/special-
reports/2026/20260506-powering-reliability-through-market-design.pdf. 
7 PJM 2026 Whitepaper at 3. 
8 Id.

4 
 
vast amounts of expertise, and the organization is capable of remarkable operational performance 
(e.g., during the recent heat dome in early July). But long-term organizational success is not 
adequately measured by its ability to manage crisis to crisis, capacity auction to capacity auction, 
or extreme weather event (summer or winter) to extreme weather event.   
 Our goals are straightforward.  We seek to equip PJM with the governance tools to (i) 
reliably plan the system and run its markets with clear, stable and transparent rules, (ii) 
improve the effectiveness of the PJM stakeholder process and (iii) strengthen PJM’s 
accountability to grid asset owners and other PJM stakeholders to restore confidence in its 
decision-making.   
In furtherance of these goals, we propose a targeted framework for the Commission’s 
consideration: 
• First, the Consolidated Transmission Owners Agreement (“CTOA”) and the PJM 
Operating Agreement (“OA”) must be amended to empower PJM to make effective 
regional planning decisions while increasing its accountability to grid asset owners. 
• Second, changes to voting rules are desperately needed. Change could take one of two 
forms – either aligning voting rules with members’ actual and measurable stake in PJM 
outcomes or full advisory voting, which, when coupled with increased PJM 
accountability, may allow PJM to leverage its knowledge of the system and the markets 
to make independent, timely and bold decisions and stick with them. 
• Third, in light of the fundamental changes happening in the industry, PJM’s stakeholder 
process needs to accelerate to meet this moment.   
• Fourth, there should be enhanced accountability for PJM, including regular third-party 
evaluations of the PJM Board’s and PJM senior management performance.   
Finally, we support a revised role for the PJM states, reflecting their role in resource 
adequacy and their desire to better understand and positively impact the stakeholder process. At 
the same time, any such change must be linked to effectuating improved outcomes in PJM, as 
measured by the above-listed objectives of achieving reliable system planning and stable, well-
functioning markets, an effective stakeholder process and measurable PJM accountability.  
Comments

5 
 
II. 
The CTOA and the OA must be amended to empower PJM’s regional transmission 
planning and enhance its accountability to asset owners. 
1. What is the status quo under the current CTOA paradigm? 
The CTOA is the foundational agreement by which the TOs collectively contracted with 
PJM to transfer control of over $80 billion of transmission assets to PJM. Under the CTOA, 
PJM is responsible for: (1) providing open-access transmission service, including processing 
transmission service and interconnection requests; (2) directing the operation of the TOs’ 
transmission facilities and monitoring/operating the bulk power system; (3) preparing the RTEP 
and the load forecast used as an input to the RTEP; and (4) conducting all planning of 
“expansions” and “enhancements” to the regional transmission grid.9 The TOs retain 
responsibility to: (1) build, finance, own, acquire, sell, or otherwise transfer assets, 
including terminating the member’s relationship with PJM; (2) maintain, repair and replace 
transmission assets; (3) identify and plan supplemental projects to address local reliability needs; 
and (4) seek FERC approval for new rules or changes to existing rules regarding the recovery of 
transmission revenue requirements, rate design and cost allocation.10   
The CTOA is unique among the PJM governing documents in establishing a demarcated and 
fundamental split of responsibilities between PJM and its TOs. Yet, the agreement is often 
ignored in discussions about PJM governance. The legal and practical reality is that it cannot be 
ignored. From the TO perspective, discussions about the future of PJM governance must start 
with the CTOA.  
 One fundamental flaw with the CTOA is that it memorializes a structure whereby the 
regional planning protocol establishing rules for regional transmission planning resides in the 
PJM OA instead of the Tariff. Pursuant to the CTOA, “Each party shall transfer to PJM, 
pursuant to this Agreement and in accordance with the Operating Agreement, the 
responsibility to prepare a Regional Transmission Expansion Plan and to provide information 
reasonably requested by PJM to prepare the Regional Transmission Expansion Plan...”11 And 
under the OA, PJM is required to obtain the approval of the PJM Members Committee prior to 
 
9See CTOA, Sections 4.1 and 6.3. 
10 CTOA, Sections 5 and 7.  
11 Id. section 4.1.4 (emphasis added).

6 
 
filing any change in its planning rules under Section 205 of the Federal Power Act (absent such 
approval, PJM is required to file under Federal Power Act Section 206 to effectuate the 
change).12 PJM has itself explained, “In the absence of such Members Committee approval, PJM 
may only propose a change to its planning rules for the Commission’s consideration using FPA 
section 206, thereby: (i) requiring PJM to first meet the higher statutory burden of demonstrating 
that an existing provision (or absence of a provision) is ‘unjust and unreasonable,’ prior to 
actually proposing the rule change for consideration; and (ii) creating an indeterminate period of 
time for Commission action on PJM’s proposed rule change.”13 This allows members to make 
decisions about RTEP rules through the OA when the underlying responsibility to plan the 
regional transmission system clearly resides with PJM under the CTOA.    
PJM is the only RTO that does not have independent Section 205 filing rights over 
transmission planning. 14 This paradigm undermines PJM’s independence to plan the grid and 
potentially hamstrings PJM from being able to pursue transmission grid initiatives due to 
stakeholder voting factions and dysfunction. Another challenge with the CTOA is that the TOs 
have no audit rights of PJM and therefore no way under the agreement to hold PJM accountable 
for its performance under the agreement. Other RTOs, including SPP and MISO, provide such 
rights to their TO members. In SPP, transmission owners have audit rights to “verify compliance 
by SPP with [the Membership] Agreement, to audit and verify transactions … and to assist 
Member[s] in complying with[]statutory and regulatory requirements” under the Membership 
Agreement.15 MISO TOs have nearly identical provisions in their Transmission Owners 
Agreement, which state that “MISO shall grant each Member, its employees or agents, external 
auditors, and federal and state regulatory authorities having jurisdiction over MISO or an Owner, 
 
12 See Operating Agreement, Section 18.6(a) (as amended). 
13 Duquesne Light Co., PJM Transmittal Letter, Docket Nos. ER24-2336-000, et al., at 2 (Jun. 21, 2024). 
14 In 2024, the Commission rejected proposed changes to the CTOA and OA that would have provided PJM 
independent planning rights and addressed identified gaps and problems with the CTOA. The Commission did not 
disagree with the underlying premise that PJM should have filing rights with respect to its RTEP rules.  See 
Duquesne Light Co., Order Rejecting Consolidated Transmission Owners Agreement Amendments and Denying 
Complaint, Docket Nos. ER24-2336-000, et al.,189 FERC ¶ 61,181 (Dec. 6, 2024).  On rehearing of that decision, 
the Commission emphasized that the “dismissal of the PJM Complaint here does not preclude a future filing 
proposing to move the RTEP Protocol from the OA to the Tariff.  The PJM Board has the authority to petition the 
Commission under FPA section 206 to modify any provision or schedule of the OA that the PJM Board believes to 
be unjust, unreasonable, or unduly discriminatory.” Duquesne Light Co., 192 FERC ¶ 61,051 at P 105 (July 14, 
2025) (emphasis added). 
15 See Southwest Power Pool, Inc., "Membership Agreement," Section 2.4 (May 1, 2004), available at: 
https://spp.org.

7 
 
such access to MISO's books and records as is necessary to verify compliance by MISO with the 
MISO Agreement and to audit and verify transactions under the MISO Agreement.”16 Nothing 
comparable exists in either the CTOA or the PJM OA, but such rights should exist.  
2. What changes should be made to the CTOA and related governing documents and how 
can they be effectuated? 
Specific changes to the CTOA and related governing documents are needed to address these 
flaws, including:  
a. Amending the CTOA to effectuate the transfer of the planning protocols from the OA 
to the PJM Tariff so that PJM has independent Section 205 filing rights with respect 
to its RTEP rules; and 
b. Incorporating audit provisions in both the CTOA and OA to monitor PJM’s 
performance and ensure compliance with its responsibilities. 
These changes would require a FERC filing and approval as part of either a Section 205 or 
Section 206-initiated proceeding.   
III. 
PJM’s voting framework must be fundamentally overhauled.   
1. What is the status quo under current PJM voting rules? 
As illustrated in the table below, the PJM of the late 1990s is radically different from the 
PJM of 2026.17  At its inception as an ISO in 1997, PJM was composed of only 10 TO members 
located in 5 states and the District of Columbia.18 Approximately thirty years later, PJM’s 
membership has risen to over 1,100 total members and 532 voting members in 13 states and the 
District of Columbia.19 The original limited membership of similar companies varied only by 
geography, and issues were largely considered from similar points of view. PJM in 2026 reflects 
states with different policy priorities and different degrees of reliance on the capacity market.

https://cdn.misoenergy.org/MISO%20TOA%20(for%20posting)47071.pdf.

PJM’s senior standing committees – the Markets and Reliability Committee and the Members 
Committee - use sector-weighted voting, with members categorized into one of five sectors with 
equal voting strength. Each of the five sectors has 20% of the vote and a proposal must achieve 
2/3 approval from the sectors to pass.  PJM’s sector voting structure was designed to ensure that 
no one group could “disproportionately dominate” the stakeholder decision-making and voting 
processes. Yet the PJM voting structure when applied to today’s membership composition no 
longer works to produce effective outcomes.  
Below are two real-world examples of anomalies and inefficiencies in the PJM voting 
process that impede resolution of critical issues: 
• Critical Issue Fast Path (“CIFP”) process for Large Loads: This stakeholder process 
was initiated by PJM to develop rules around the important issue of the integration of 
large loads. Yet, when votes on proposals were taken in November 2025, only 118 of 520 
eligible Members participated, reflecting 24% of PJM’s total voting population. The 
Generation Owner and Other Supplier sectors had less than half of their membership in 
attendance (29% and 7% respectively), but those two sectors combined for 40% of the 
sector-weighting under PJM’s voting protocol.20 The ability of two sectors to join 
together to “sector block” a proposal from being endorsed is magnified with limited 
 
20 PJM Operating Agreement 8.4.

9 
 
voting participation and represents a meaningful flaw in the voting process. In the case of 
the CIFP vote, no proposal was ultimately endorsed on this key substantive matter.  
• End of Life Transmission Planning: In 2019, PJM initiated a stakeholder process to 
establish criteria that would apply to all transmission projects seeking to resolve “end of 
life” drivers on PJM Tariff transmission assets.21 The process culminated in a vote at the 
Members Committee where a proposal seeking to transfer responsibility for “end of life” 
decision-making away from the TOs and to PJM received a 69% sector-weighted 
supermajority vote. This proposal was brought by a coalition of “joint stakeholders” that 
do not have any responsibility for the ownership, operation or planning of transmission 
facilities. Ultimately, the member-endorsed proposal was filed at FERC and was opposed 
by PJM itself, who explained to FERC that the members filing conflicted with the rights 
of the Transmission Owners under the CTOA.22 This is a perfect example of a misaligned 
stakeholder process that wasted resources and produced a poor (and ultimately FERC-
rejected) outcome.   
2. What changes should be made to PJM’s current voting rules and how can these changes 
be effectuated? 
We present two types of potential solutions to revise the current PJM voting structure.  
The first category would involve implementing a different weighting so that votes are based 
on a member’s actual level of interest in PJM and its stake in PJM outcomes. The second 
category would simply make all voting advisory. In PSEG’s view, this second approach will 
not be as effective if pursued in isolation and, given the increased authority accorded to PJM 
under this scenario, should be accompanied by meaningful changes to enhance PJM’s 
accountability and clearly delineate responsibilities.   
a. Changes to the voting structure to reflect members’ actual economic and operational 
stake in PJM outcomes  
 
21 See PJM Interconnection, LLC, "Issue Details: Transparency and End of Life Planning," PJM Issue Tracking ID: 
23b82425-6796-4b0c-8c4a-5ff9b6b5f061, available at: https://www.pjm.com/committees-and-groups/issue-
tracking/issue-tracking-details.aspx?Issue=23b82425-6796-4b0c-8c4a-5ff9b6b5f061. 
22 PJM Interconnection L.L.C., 176 FERC ¶ 61,053 (2021).

10 
 
PJM’s current voting rules mean that asset owners with responsibility for customer reliability 
and long-lived assets in the ground have a significantly diluted vote.23 Yet, several states have 
implicitly recognized the importance of their utilities’ role in the PJM voting process. For 
example, last year, New Jersey enacted a law that requires the four electric utilities in the state 
that “transmit and distribute electricity to end users within the State” to submit an annual voting 
report to the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities that lists all recorded votes cast by the utilities, 
describes the context of the votes and explains how each vote “furthers the State’s goals of 
promoting affordability, reliability and sustainability of electricity production, consumption and 
conservation ….”24 No other PJM voting member with interests in New Jersey (including 
generators located in the state, retail default service providers, municipal electric utilities or the 
New Jersey Division of Rate Counsel) is required to report their votes to the Board of Public 
Utilities. This requirement, which has been adopted by New Jersey, Maryland and Virginia and is 
under consideration by Illinois and Pennsylvania, underscores the unique role of the utility in 
PJM voting and only underscores the mismatch between the nature of the utility interest and the 
actual ability to influence a PJM vote.25    
There are several different voting changes that could be pursued, all of which would involve 
modification of the PJM OA, to align voting weight with “skin in the game.” One such option 
would be to match voting interest with member responsibilities under the default cost allocation 
methodology contained in Section 15.2.2 of the OA. These rules assign a share of member 
default costs to market participants based on their respective market activity (gross billings).26  
Under these rules, PSEG and other larger market participants face the potential for significant 
default allocations and must account for such risk in their risk management plans. Yet, our vote 
in the stakeholder process is disconnected from these risks that we bear. Another option would be 
to weigh TO votes more heavily for votes involving transmission planning rules. A final option is 
a bicameral voting structure that would count a member’s vote on both a per capita basis and an 
 
23 Despite being a major asset owner with an obligation under state law to provide safe, adequate, and proper service 
and an obligation under the PJM governing documents to maintain, repair, and replace transmission assets for 
reliability, PSEG’s vote constitutes about 1.5% of the total vote in PJM senior standing committees and only 0.4% of 
the vote in the lower committees. 
24  N.J.S.A. 48:2-16.5.  
25 See Maryland House Bill 121 and Senate Bill 37; Virginia House Bill 84; New Jersey Assembly Bill 5463; IL 
House Bill 1802; Pennsylvania House Bill 1599. 
26 See Section 15.2.2 of the PJM Operating Agreement.

11 
 
asset ownership basis. Under this approach, the asset ownership component of the vote would 
reflect MWs of generation capacity, ownership of transmission assets and/or MWs of load owned 
or controlled by members. This structure would appropriately recognize the operational and 
financial stake of the members in PJM’s voting process but would at the same time be balanced 
by a per capita allocation.27      
b.  Alternatively, PJM could consider adopting advisory stakeholder voting 
  
We recognize that other RTOs/ISOs employ full stakeholder advisory voting and that 
PJM already uses it for certain matters falling within the PJM Tariff such as RPM capacity 
market rules. For example, MISO operates under an advisory stakeholder process “that provides 
input to MISO on the regional system plan and a range of market- and tariff-related issues and 
policy initiatives.”28 Similarly, voting in the New England Power Pool (“NEPOOL”) stakeholder 
process for ISO New England (“ISO-NE”) is advisory; however, if an alternative NEPOOL 
proposal meets a particular voting threshold, “then ISO-NE must include in its Section 205 filing 
a description of the alternative proposal” under the “jump ball” provision.29 If advisory voting 
were to be implemented in PJM, it would shift the ultimate responsibility for decision-making 
onto PJM and create a structure whereby PJM could independently design and propose Tariff 
revisions to the FERC on all issues under its purview. While one may legitimately question 
whether this type of voting has worked with respect to the RPM capacity market rules, we 
understand that, at least in theory, full advisory voting could help to embolden PJM to act 
independently and more decisively. Because this approach would provide more authority to PJM 
it must be accompanied by enhanced accountability, including for the PJM Board, so that 
members have confidence in the decisions PJM is making. 
 
 
 
27  Comments of the PSEG Companies on PJM’s Order No. 719 Compliance filing in ER09-1063 at 11 (June 26, 
2009). 
28 NESCOE February 19, 2021White Paper on “Governance Structure and Practices in the FERC Jurisdictional 
ISOs/RTOs” prepared by Exeter at Section 4.3. available at Governance Structure and Practices in the FERC 
Jurisdictional ISOs/RTOs | NESCOE 
29 Id. at Section 3.4.

12 
 
IV. 
The PJM stakeholder process should be reformed to accelerate the speed of decision-
making.    
We agree with FERC that the current PJM stakeholder process is too slow and subject to the 
obstructive agendas of various stakeholders. The inability to coalesce on issues in the PJM 
stakeholder process has resulted in tremendous inefficiencies and in some cases a complete 
failure to act at all. One such example, referenced above, is the CIFP process to develop large 
load integration rules, which occurred between August 2025 and November 2025. Despite 11 
stakeholder meetings, no proposal was endorsed by the members for consideration by the PJM 
Board. This lack of action in turn resulted in direct federal and state intervention in PJM 
decision-making, specifically the January 2026 National Energy Dominance Council and the 
thirteen PJM state agreement memorializing the “Statement of Principles Regarding PJM.30  
Modest changes can be implemented in the short term that will expedite decision-making in 
the stakeholder process, and we offer a few for consideration: 
• Upfront identification of purpose and system benefits of all stakeholder proposals (would 
require revisions to PJM Manual 34): Solution proposals offered by stakeholders should 
contain a clear purpose - tied to the defined scope of the stakeholder process at issue - 
and should explain the measurable benefits that will result if the proposal is endorsed. If 
the proposal is lacking in any of these respects, PJM should require that the proposal, 
either be removed from consideration or changed to satisfy these criteria before a vote is 
taken.     
• Member-only proposal submissions (would require revisions to PJM Manual 34):  
PJM should strongly consider limiting stakeholder proposal submission to members or 
requiring that at least one member be a co-sponsor to a proposal. Non-member 
stakeholders may continue to participate and be heard in stakeholder meetings - and can 
seek to influence the content of proposals - but should not be permitted to sponsor 
proposals without at least one member also attached to the proposal. Otherwise, non-
member stakeholders are allowed a significant benefit of membership without bearing 
 
30 See Statement of Principles signed by the NEDC and the PJM Governors (available at statement-principles-
regarding-pjm.pdf)

13 
 
any of the responsibilities that come along with membership. That asymmetry produces 
poor outcomes and is also highly inefficient.   
• More frequent use of the CIFP process: 
PJM crafted the CIFP mechanism for use on substantive issues that are “...extremely 
difficult to resolve, within the normal CBIR Stakeholder process...in extraordinary 
circumstances (broad impact to markets or significant reliability issue).”31 If 
accompanied by PJM adoption of new rules that better vet the content and sponsorship of 
proposals, more frequent use of the CIFP process could facilitate efficient and effective 
engagement on critical issues in a structured and time-bounded manner.  
V. 
Reforms are critical to enhance PJM’s accountability and ensure defensible, durable 
outcomes.  Specific to resource adequacy, additional clarity is needed to delineate 
responsibilities.  
Accountability 
PJM’s 2026 Whitepaper on potential market design reforms captures the gravity of the 
resource adequacy problem at hand. At the same time, the whitepaper fails to identify concrete, 
timely and actionable solutions. Rather, the white paper merely notes that relevant decisions on 
future market design “belong to the people and institutions with democratic accountability for 
their consequences – to state regulators and legislatures, to FERC, to consumers and the 
advocates who represent them.”32 Given PJM’s status as the independent FERC-approved entity 
responsible for the reliability of a grid that serves over 65 million customers, its choice to refrain 
from making a recommendation on a path forward feels inadequate.   
Order No. 719 requires each RTO or ISO to demonstrate “that it has in place, or will adopt, 
practices and procedures to ensure that its board of directors is responsive to customers and other 
stakeholders.”33 In compliance with this requirement, PJM must make difficult, and at times 
unpopular, decisions and then explain those decisions to its stakeholders and stand by those 
decisions.  
 
31 See PJM Manual 34: PJM Stakeholder Process (Sept. 25, 2025). 
32 See PJM 2026 Whitepaper at 3. 
33 See Order 719 at P 477.

14 
 
There are corporate governance principles that PJM could adopt to promote accountability 
and responsiveness from its leadership to its stakeholders. For example, PJM should utilize a 
third party to regularly evaluate the performance of its Board and its executive leadership team, 
and its Board should in turn regularly evaluate the performance and effectiveness of its senior 
leadership. There are several questions that will need to be answered to effectively evaluate 
PJM’s performance, including: (1) what are the appropriate metrics to be used to measure 
accountability and responsiveness; (2) which entity is responsible for conducting that 
measurement; (3) where should those requirements be documented; and (4) what are the 
repercussions for failing to meet those performance metrics. However, the answers to these 
questions are secondary to beginning in earnest an effort to increase organizational 
accountability.   
In its compliance filing in response to Order No. 719, PJM pointed to the existence of the 
Governance Assessment Special Team (“GAST”) stakeholder forum as a demonstration of PJM’s 
commitment to considering further enhancements (beyond the requirements of Order No. 719) to 
its stakeholder and governance processes.34 The GAST was used to examine the concerns of PJM 
membership regarding governance and stakeholder processes and to develop solutions. Under 
that process, PJM implemented both the Consensus-Based Issue Resolution (“CBIR”) process 
and the Stakeholder Process Forum to more efficiently engage stakeholders.35 GAST also 
implemented the Enhanced Liaison Committee to address important and divisive issues.36  PJM 
should employ a forum comparable to GAST to work with its stakeholders to develop 
accountability metrics. That forum could also be used to examine whether the existing 
requirements for PJM Board participation remain appropriate, including the two-year cooling-off 
period on material affiliation with a market participant and the lack of a residency or regional 
connection requirement, or whether they should instead be modified or strengthened.37

15 
 
Defined Roles for Resource Adequacy 
 
Enhancing PJM’s accountability will restore confidence in its decision-making at this critical 
time where it must work with its stakeholders and the PJM states to tackle resource adequacy and 
the rapid integration of large load customers. PJM has indirect responsibility for resource 
adequacy through its use of market pricing signals to incent the addition of new generation and 
to retain existing resources. However, PJM is not an integrated resource planner and therefore 
does not plan generation.  
By contrast, the PJM states do have authority to address resource adequacy through the 
planning of generation and a vested interest in ensuring that, to the extent they continue to rely 
on PJM’s markets, rules for those markets are transparent and will procure sufficient supply to 
maintain reliability. There is a pressing need for clarity on the respective responsibilities between 
PJM and the states on resource adequacy, and discussions should occur as to how PJM and the 
states – with support from asset owners with responsibility for reliability - will work together to 
obtain this clarity. Those discussions need to happen now.   
PJM, its states and the TOs have recently collaborated on load forecasting improvements, 
which will involve, among other things, use of a third party consultant to verify large load 
forecast data, review by the states of such data and formalized involvement by the states in the 
overall load forecasting process to ensure state policies are accurately reflected in the forecast.38  
Appropriately involving the states in a fulsome way in load forecasting will help to ensure a 
more accurate and defensible work product. PJM and its states could adopt a similarly productive 
approach to resource adequacy, and one way to advance progress would be through the use of a 
properly-bounded state advisory committee, such as exists in SPP and the ISO-NE, with clearly-
defined roles and responsibilities.

16 
 
VI. 
Conclusion  
Getting the rules right on PJM governance is critical and the time for action is now. Reforms 
must be focused on changing and improving PJM’s decision-making and providing PJM with the 
tools to effectuate sustainable outcomes that will ensure long-term system reliability. PSEG’s 
proposed solutions – providing PJM with filing rights over transmission planning rules, changing 
voting in a meaningful way, making stakeholder processes more efficient and enhancing PJM 
accountability for its decisions – are intended to satisfy these objectives.
